chapter: The Bride Ran Away. The Groom Had No Idea.
subtitle: 新娘跑了，新郎还不知道
sentences: I landed in a novel in the middle of drugging the bride's tea.
I had only poured in half the powder when someone behind me asked, "Jiang Mingyue, what are you putting in my cup?"
My hand jerked. The paper packet tipped, dusting my sleeve with white powder.
In the bronze mirror was a face almost unfairly beautiful.
The bride wore a red wedding gown embroidered with gold. Her phoenix hairpin was still sitting crooked, and she was watching me in the mirror.
She didn't call anyone or cry. She simply nudged the empty teacup beside her a little farther away.
I knew that face.
Wen Li, the heroine of The Marquis's Darling.
I'd stayed up the night before to finish the book.

It was three in the morning by the time I reached the end, and I still wrote an eight-hundred-word comment. My main point was simple: if Xie Linzhou was so good at making people miserable, why hadn't anyone sent him off to work in the fields?
Then I opened my eyes and found myself in the body of his vicious cousin.
In the original novel, Jiang Mingyue was hopelessly in love with Xie Linzhou, the Marquis of Dingbei's heir, and couldn't bear the thought of his marrying Wen Li.
Today, she was supposed to drug the bride at the Wen residence, make her collapse during the wedding ceremony, then accuse her of having an affair.
The scheme would be exposed, and Xie Linzhou would have her beaten twenty times with a wooden board.
By Chapter Seven, she'd be banished to the family shrine. By Chapter Nineteen, she'd die in a fire.
And here I was, still holding the packet of powder.
"Say something."
Wen Li turned around.
"What is that?"
"I don't know what's in it."
I tightened my grip on the little paper packet.
"But I know it's no tonic."
Her brows drew together.
"And you actually admit it?"
"Because you haven't drunk it yet."
I picked up a lidded tea bowl, poured in the tea I had just tampered with, and closed the lid tightly.
"I'm keeping this.
Have someone examine it if you want. I won't touch it. As for everything I did before..."
"Before?"
She caught the word and let out a short, mirthless laugh.
"Miss Jiang, last month you pushed me into a lake.
Two days ago, you put a snake in my courtyard. Yesterday, you called me a social climber in front of a whole street of people.
And today you tried to drug me.
I wonder what you'll come up with tomorrow."
I opened my mouth.
Finding myself inside a novel might explain how I'd got here. It didn't erase the harm Jiang Mingyue had done.
To the people she'd hurt, I was still Jiang Mingyue. Who was inside her body made no difference.
"What I did before was wrong,"
I said. "I understand why you don't trust me.
I'll keep the tea as evidence."
Wen Li studied me for a moment. "Weren't you here to make me miss the auspicious hour?"
"Yes, I did."
"And you've changed your mind?"
"I have.
I finally realized Xie Linzhou isn't worth it."
Something in her expression changed at last.
"Two days ago, you called him the finest man in the world."
"Two days ago, I had terrible taste."
"In just two days?"
"Sometimes you come to your senses all at once."
I meant it. She looked as if I had said something astonishing.
A smile tugged at the corner of her mouth, then disappeared.
I took the chance to ask,
"Did Xie Linzhou threaten you again last night?"
Wen Li said nothing.
"Did he tell you you weren't allowed to go anywhere without his permission?"
Her hand froze on the phoenix crown.
"How do you know that?"
If only she knew how much more I remembered.
One day, he would tell her, "Run once and I'll catch you once," and expect her to mistake it for romance.
Readers of the original novel called it 'forced love.' I couldn't see much love in the forcing.
"Just a guess,"
I said. "Do you want to marry him?"
The room fell silent.
Outside, the house was bustling with preparations for the wedding procession.
Someone was counting wedding pastries in the courtyard, the wedding attendant was urging the bride to fix her makeup, and drums and gongs sounded from the street.
"My father is being held at the Ministry of Punishments,"
Wen Li said at last. "Xie Linzhou promised to speak for him after the wedding."
I remembered that part.
Her father had recently been jailed over an old case involving relief grain sent to Beihe three years ago.
The original novel said he had embezzled the grain. Xie Linzhou claimed he could save him if Wen Li married into his family.
But when her father was released in Chapter Five, the novel explained it in one line: "The young lord had his ways."
I'd remembered every scene where the leads argued and kissed. Now that a life depended on the details, I couldn't recall a single useful one.
"Did he promise you anything concrete?"
I asked.
"Did he put it in writing?
Who is supposed to plead for your father tomorrow?"
"No."
"So he gets you through his front door first, and everything else is just 'we'll see' later?"
Wen Li looked out the window. She didn't argue.
"If you don't want to marry him," I whispered, "I'll help you leave."
At last, she turned back.
"You'll help me?"
"Don't look at me like that.
At least I know which wedding sedan you're meant to ride in today."
"Why would you help me?"
"Because I don't want to die."
That was only half the truth.
The other half was that I couldn't stand the thought of Wen Li being shut away for the rest of her life, as she was in the novel, all because a man knew how to say the right things.
Wen Li held out her hand.
"Lend me your family's carriage pass."
"How did you know I brought a carriage pass?"
"Your maid said at the door that your carriage was waiting in the east alley."
"You're leaving by the east alley?"
"I need to get out of the Wen residence first."
It was a very precise answer.
She hadn't said she was leaving the city. She hadn't said where she would go next, either.
I was too pleased with myself to hear the difference.
Half an incense stick later, I was sitting at her dressing table with her phoenix crown on my head.
The red wedding gown was heavy, and the waist was painfully tight.
Every breath seemed to say, You've really got yourself into it now.
"Wen Li." I stared at the mirror. "When did you decide I was going to take your place in the wedding sedan?"
Behind the screen came the soft rustle of clothes being changed.
"When you offered to help."
"So you weren't convinced by a word I said?"
"I was convinced."
"By which part?"
"You were willing to stay behind for me."
I nearly choked.
"I never said I'd go that far!"
Wen Li emerged wearing the plain blue-green clothes of a Jiang-family maid, her hair fastened with a single wooden pin.
She had even smudged ash on her face. She looked like an unfortunate girl sent running errands before dawn.
I asked her, "Do you really want to escape that badly?"
"I've tried three times."
The first time, she had slipped out through the Wen residence's back gate, only to be brought back that night.
The second time, she had tried to reach her uncle in the west of the city, but Xie Linzhou's men had stopped her at a crossroads.
The third time, a maid who carried a letter for her had disappeared for two days. When the girl returned, she refused to leave the house again.
Wen Li told me all this calmly, as if she were reporting the weather.
"Why didn't you tell someone sooner?"
I asked.
"Who was I supposed to tell?"
I had no answer.
She took a step toward me.
"Jiang Mingyue, you can still change your mind.
The wedding attendant hasn't come in yet. I can change back."
I looked at the wedding gown in the mirror and remembered the tea I'd nearly made her drink.
"Forget it,"
I said. "I owe you, anyway.

But let's make three things clear. First, I won't go through with the wedding ceremony. Second, you have to find a way to get me out. Third, if you have any other plans, you have to tell me beforehand."
"I can't promise the first one."
"What?"
"The marquis's household has never cared much about being reasonable.
I'll do what I can to make sure they discover you're not me before the ceremony."
Strangely, I felt better after hearing that.
At least she wasn't making promises she couldn't keep.
"What about the second?"
"I'll come back for you."
"And the third?"
Wen Li looked at me for a moment before answering,
"I'll try."
"Wen Li!"
She smiled, but it lasted only until three soft taps sounded at the rear window.
Wen Li turned toward the window. For a heartbeat, her expression tightened.
"I'll see if the wind has blown the window open," she told me.
The window was shut. There was no wind outside.
I was about to ask a question, but she had already slipped behind the screen.
A latch clicked softly, followed by the brush of a cloth bundle against the window frame. By the time she returned, the rear window was shut again.
Wen Li came back holding a plain, worn cloth bundle. She also drew a sheet of paper from her sleeve.
"This is my written refusal of the marriage,"
she said. "I wrote two copies last night. I've kept one; take this one with you."
I unfolded the paper.
It said she had never freely consented to the marriage. At the bottom was a bright red fingerprint.
"Will Xie Linzhou accept it?"
"No."
"Then what good is it?"
"So he can't tell everyone I married him happily."
I folded the paper and slipped it into my sleeve.
In that moment, she felt more real to me than the heroine who had spent the whole novel crying.
The wedding attendant called from outside, "The auspicious hour is nearly here!"
Wen Li started for the door, then turned back.
"There's powder on your sleeve."
I looked down. Sure enough, there was a little white dust.
She wiped it off with a handkerchief and tucked the stained cloth into my embroidered pouch.
"Don't throw that away,"
she said. "If you ever deny what you did, this is evidence."
"You still think I'll go back on my word?"
"Yes."
She said it without the slightest hesitation.
Part of me wanted to be annoyed. The other part wanted to laugh.
By the time I looked up, Wen Li had left the courtyard with the Jiang-family carriage driver, carrying the old cloth bundle and my family's carriage pass.

Before I left, I put the sealed tea bowl, the paper packet holding the remaining powder, and the powder-stained handkerchief into a small cloth bag and gave it to Chuntao, who had come with me. The sight of me in a wedding gown made her turn pale. I sent her back to the Jiang residence to tell my mother what had happened, fetch a change of clothes, and meet me at the marquis's residence.
Then I lowered the red bridal veil and, for the first time in my life, prayed in earnest: Xie Linzhou, please don't love your cousin too much. And please don't hate her too much, either.
Either would be dangerous.
The bridal sedan took a long, winding route through the city.
At the marquis's residence, I waited nearly another half hour in a side room. Only when someone called out that the auspicious hour had arrived did they lead me into the wedding hall.
The music stopped. Guests crowded along both sides.
Through the veil, I could see only the red carpet and a pair of black boots.
"A-Li."
Xie Linzhou took my hand.
"I won't hold last night against you anymore."
He gripped my hand so tightly my wrist bones ached.
I put up with it for two breaths. Then I snapped.
"Xie Linzhou, let go."
The wedding hall fell silent.
His hand went still.
When the red veil came off, I finally saw Xie Linzhou's face.
He was undeniably handsome. I was equally desperate to snatch back the veil and hide beneath it.
"Jiang Mingyue?"
"Cousin."
I managed a smile.
"Congratulations on your wedding."
"Where is Wen Li?"
"She had something to take care of, so she left."
"What sort of thing?"
"...Does not wanting to get married count?"
His gaze slid from my face to my sleeve.
I suddenly remembered the letter in my sleeve and tried to pull away. Too late.
He snatched out the paper, skimmed it, and his face darkened.
"Does she think a piece of paper can end this marriage?"
"At least she's made herself clear."
"I've had men watching the west and south gates for some time."
Xie Linzhou crumpled the paper in his fist.
"She failed to get away before. She won't get away this time, either."
A chill went through me.
She had never said she was leaving the city.
Only now did that occur to me.
Xie Linzhou signaled to his personal guards. Men immediately took their places at the wedding hall doors.
The guests had heard everything. They pretended not to notice, though curiosity was practically shining in their eyes.
"Who helped her?"
Xie Linzhou asked.
"I did."
"You alone?"
I hesitated.
The three taps at the rear window came back to me.
"I don't know."
It was the truth. Xie Linzhou clearly didn't believe me.
His hand closed around his sword hilt. He had barely pushed the blade an inch from its sheath when a guard came rushing in.
"Young Lord!
The Ministry of Punishments has just received a formal complaint."
Xie Linzhou didn't move.
"Who submitted it?"
"Miss Wen.
She says the marquis's private accounts don't match the official records for the Beihe relief grain from three years ago. She also submitted an old ledger."
Xie Linzhou let go of his sword at once.
For the first time, I saw him genuinely lose his composure.
It wasn't anger.
It was the look of a man who had just realized, half an hour too late, what he had lost.
"Where did she get the ledger?"
he demanded.
The guard lowered his head.
"They say it came from your study, Young Lord."
Whispers spread among the guests.
Xie Linzhou looked at me as if he finally understood why I was standing here in a wedding gown.
I understood, too.
Wen Li had never planned to go through the west or south gates.
While Xie Linzhou watched the roads out of the city, she had gone straight to the Ministry of Punishments.
She hadn't left me at the wedding simply to escape the marriage. She had needed Xie Linzhou to waste his time here.
And she hadn't told me a thing.
Another household steward hurried in.
"Someone from the Ministry of Punishments is here. They've accepted the complaint and the ledger.
They want you to explain where the old ledger came from, Young Lord. They've also sent word that no account books connected to the old case are to be altered or destroyed."
Xie Linzhou slid his sword back into its sheath, quietly ordered his guards to watch me for the time being, and left with his men.
Before I could relax, Chuntao pushed through the crowd with a bundle of clothes in her arms.
She was pale and breathless. The sight of me still dressed as a bride almost made her cry.
"Miss, your mother says you must come home at once."
"What now?"
"The Jiang Trading House is named in that ledger, too."
I stared at the red wedding silks scattered across the floor and realized that the wedding might be the smallest of my problems today.
translations: 我穿书的时候，正往新娘的茶里下药。
药粉才倒了一半，身后就有人问：“姜明月，你往我杯子里放了什么？”
我手一抖，纸包一歪，袖口立刻沾了层白粉。
铜镜里映出一张漂亮得过分的脸。
新娘穿着绣金线的红嫁衣，发间的凤钗还没戴稳，正从镜子里看着我。
她没有叫人，也没有哭，只是将手边那只空茶盏推得远了些。
温梨，《侯爷的掌心娇》的女主。
这本书是我昨晚熬夜看完的。
看完已经凌晨三点，我还在评论区写了八百字，中心思想只有一句：谢临舟这么会折腾人，怎么没人把他送去种地？
没想到一睁眼，我成了他那个恶毒表妹。
原著的姜明月痴恋定北侯世子谢临舟，最看不惯他要娶温梨。
今天，她会在温家给新娘下药，让温梨在喜堂上昏倒，再诬陷她与人私通。
结果阴谋败露，被谢临舟打了二十板子。
第七章送进家庙，第十九章葬身火海。
而现在，药包还在我手里。
我拿过桌上的带盖茶盅，把刚动过的那杯茶倒进去，盖严了盖，
你要找人查也行，我不动它。至于以前的事……”
她捕捉到这个词，笑了一声，
“姜姑娘，上个月你推我进湖里，
前天往我院里放蛇，昨天当着满街的人骂我是攀高枝。
我倒想知道，明天还有什么新花样。”
有些事情可以怪穿书，已经做过的坏事却不能。
那些遭殃的人只知道姜明月，谁在她身体里根本不重要。
我说，“你现在不信也正常。
今日这杯茶，我会留下做证据。”
温梨盯着我看了片刻，忽然问：“你今天来，不是为了让我错过吉时？”
她的眼神终于有了点变化：
“你前日还说他是天下最好的男子。”
我说得很认真，她却像是听到了什么稀奇事，
唇角微微一弯，又很快收住。
“昨晚谢临舟是不是又威胁你了？”
“他说，没他的允许，你哪儿也不准去？”
这回，她的手停在了凤冠上。
还知道他以后会说‘你跑一次，我就抓一次’，然后把抓人说成深情。
原著读者把这叫强制爱，我只能看见那个‘强制’。
有人在院里数喜饼，喜娘催着补妆，街上传来断断续续的锣鼓声。
温梨终于说，“谢临舟答应，成亲后替他求情。”
温父最近因三年前的北河赈粮旧案下狱。
原著说他贪污，谢临舟说只要温梨嫁过来，便能救他。
但第五章温父出狱时，书里只写了‘世子自有办法’。
我忽然发现，自己记住的全是男女主吵架亲嘴的情节，真到了要用的时候，一个能救人的细节都没有。
“那不就是先把人骗进府，剩下的以后再说？”
“你若不想嫁，”我压低声音，“我帮你走。”
我至少认识你今天要坐的花轿。”
另一半是，我实在不想看温梨像原著那样，为了一句好听话被关上一辈子。
“你的丫鬟在门口说，马车停在东巷。”
没有说离城，也没有说接下来去哪儿。
我当时只顾着高兴，还没听出区别。
半炷香后，我头戴凤冠，坐在她的梳妆镜前。
我每呼吸一次都觉得有人在提醒我：你真的把自己卖进去了。
“温梨。”我望着镜子，“你什么时候想到让我替你坐花轿的？”
屏风后传来换衣服的轻响。
“所以你压根不是被我说动的？”
温梨出来时已经换成了姜府丫鬟的青布衣裳，头发只用一根木簪挽住。
她还给自己脸上抹了点灰，看起来像个大清早被抓来跑腿的倒霉姑娘。
第一次，她从温府后门出去，当夜被送回来。
第二次，想去城西投奔舅父，在路口被谢临舟的人拦下。
第三次，替她送信的丫鬟失踪了两天，回来后再也不肯出府。
她说这些话时很平静，像是在报今天下过几场雨。
“姜明月，你现在反悔，还来得及。
喜娘没进门，我可以换回来。”
我看着镜里那身红嫁衣，想起自己方才险些送进她嘴里的药。
我说，“反正我也欠你一笔。
可是先说好，第一，我不拜堂；第二，你得想办法把我弄出来；第三，有别的安排，必须提前告诉我。”
我只能尽量让你在拜堂前被认出来。”
她说完，我反倒放心了些。
她笑了。那笑意很短，转眼又被窗外三声轻敲打断。
温梨回头看向后窗，神情有一瞬间绷紧。
她对我说：“我去看看风是不是把窗吹开了。”
窗户关得好好的，外头也没风。
我本想问，她却已经绕到屏风后。
我听见窗闩轻轻一响，接着是布包擦过窗框的动静。等她再出来，后窗已经关好了。
温梨出来时，手里多了个不起眼的旧布包，袖中还抽出一张纸。
她说，“昨夜写的。我留了一份，这份你带着。”
上面写明婚事并非她自愿应允，末尾按着鲜红的指印。
“让他不能替我说，我是高高兴兴嫁过去的。”
那一刻，我突然觉得她比原著里那个不停掉眼泪的女主真实得多。
喜娘在外面喊：“吉时快到了！”
温梨向门口走去，临走前又回头：
我低头一看，果然有点白。
她拿帕子替我擦净，连帕子一并塞进我的绣袋。
她说，“你以后若想抵赖，这是证据。”
等我抬头，温梨已拎着旧布包，拿着姜府车牌，跟着姜府车夫出了院门。
出门前，我将封好的茶盅、装着余下药粉的纸包和那块沾了药粉的帕子一并塞进小布包，交给随我来的春桃收着。她看见我穿着嫁衣，脸都白了。我让她先回姜府给母亲报信，顺便给我取身能换的衣裳，再赶去侯府。
随后我扣下红盖头，第一次认真祈祷：谢临舟最好别太爱我这个表妹，也别太恨我。
花轿在城里绕了一大圈。
到了侯府，我又在偏厅等了近半个时辰，直到外头有人喊吉时，才被扶进喜堂。
鼓乐停了，宾客挤在两边。
我隔着盖头只能看见红毡和一双黑靴。
他的手劲很大，攥得我腕骨发疼。
红盖头被掀起时，我看见谢临舟的脸。
很好看，也确实很想让人当场把盖头抢回去。
他的目光从我脸上落到袖口。
我忽然想起那张退婚书，急忙往后缩，却迟了一步。
他将纸抽出去，扫了一眼，脸色渐沉。
“她前几次没走成，这次也走不成。”
谢临舟朝亲卫使了个眼色，立刻有人守住喜堂的门。
宾客都听见了动静，装作没看见，眼睛却一个比一个亮。
后窗的三声敲击忽然在耳边响起来。
这句是实话，谢临舟显然不信。
他握住剑柄，刚将剑推出一寸，外头就有护卫跑进来。
她说侯府私账与三年前北河赈粮的官册对不上，还送上一本旧账簿。”
谢临舟的手立刻松开了剑。
我第一次在他脸上看见真正的失态。
是他花了半个时辰才想通，自己到底丢了什么。
谢临舟看了看我，像终于明白我是怎么被送到这里的。
温梨没打算去西门、南门。
她让谢临舟盯着出城的路，自己转头去了刑部。
她留下我，不只是为了逃婚，也是为了让谢临舟在这里把时间耗完。
“刑部来人，已收下状纸和账册，
请世子过去说明旧册来历。还传了话，府里与旧案有关的账册暂时不得毁改。”
谢临舟收好剑，低声吩咐亲卫暂且看住我，随后带人走了。
我还没来得及松气，春桃就抱着包袱从宾客后头挤过来。
她跑得脸色煞白，见我还穿着嫁衣，差点哭出来。
我望着满地红绸，终于明白，刚才那场婚礼恐怕只是今天最小的一桩麻烦。

annotations.explain: in the middle of + doing / 名词，描述动作进行中。
annotations.example: I was in the middle of dinner when she called.

annotations.phrase: I had only poured in half the powder when
annotations.explain: had poured 表示相对于问话已先发生的动作；when 引出紧接发生的事件。
annotations.example: I had barely sat down when the phone rang.

annotations.explain: unfairly 在此是夸张的主观评价，不是实际不公正。
annotations.example: The garden looked almost unfairly beautiful.

annotations.explain: 用以概括较长评论的主旨；不再是旧版 boiled down to。
annotations.example: My main point is simple: we need more time.

annotations.phrase: found myself in the body of
annotations.meaning: 发现自己进入了……的身体
annotations.explain: find oneself + 地点/状态，表达醒来后意外发现的处境。
annotations.example: I found myself in a strange room.

annotations.explain: bear the thought of + 名词/动名词，表达难以接受的想象。
annotations.example: I couldn't bear the thought of losing it.

annotations.phrase: accuse her of having an affair
annotations.explain: accuse sb of + 名词/动名词，表示提出指控，不代表指控属实。
annotations.example: They accused him of lying.

annotations.explain: draw together 描写眉头收紧，与原版 twitched 有所不同。
annotations.example: His brows drew together in confusion.

annotations.explain: actually 在问句中突出惊讶；旧版 have the nerve to 已不在正文。
annotations.example: Did you actually say that?

annotations.explain: 这里指不再动证物，不能继续把旧版 tamper with 当作原文注释。
annotations.example: I won't touch the files until you return.

annotations.explain: 人物辱骂的措辞，不能当作经证实的事实。
annotations.example: He called her a social climber.

annotations.meaning: 并不消除已经造成的伤害
annotations.explain: explain 原因与 erase 后果是两层事情。
annotations.example: An apology doesn't erase the harm.

annotations.explain: 古代婚嫁语境中的吉利时辰，是文化词。
annotations.example: They chose an auspicious date for the ceremony.

annotations.explain: worth it 评价付出与回报是否相称。
annotations.example: The long wait is not worth it.

annotations.explain: come to one's senses 是固定表达。
annotations.example: He came to his senses and apologized.

annotations.explain: mistake A for B 表示误认；替换旧 pass it off as。
annotations.example: She mistook the stranger for her teacher.

annotations.explain: could not see much + 名词表达对某种说法持怀疑态度。
annotations.example: I couldn't see much value in the plan.

annotations.explain: bustle with 是热闹、忙碌的画面描写。
annotations.example: The kitchen was bustling with activity.

annotations.explain: speak for sb 在这里是代人说情，不能保证成功。
annotations.example: She promised to speak for her colleague.

annotations.explain: 文化与案件背景词，不代表贪污指控已获证实。
annotations.example: The records listed the relief grain delivered that year.

annotations.explain: put sth in writing 表示有文件可核对。
annotations.example: Please put the offer in writing.

annotations.explain: leave 此处不保证离开整座城市；这是后续伏笔。
annotations.example: I'll help you leave the building safely.

annotations.explain: 说了一部分真话而省略关键内容。
annotations.example: That explanation was only half the truth.

annotations.explain: pass 为通行凭据，不是动词。
annotations.example: Show your pass at the gate.

annotations.explain: too + adj + to do，后者因为程度而未发生。
annotations.example: He was too excited to sleep.

annotations.phrase: You've really got yourself into it now
annotations.meaning: 这下真把自己卷进去了
annotations.explain: get oneself into sth 在这里带自嘲，不涉及买卖。
annotations.example: I've got myself into a mess.

annotations.explain: stay behind 是留下不走；旧的 in my place 并未出现在新版该句。
annotations.example: Could you stay behind for a minute?

annotations.explain: only to 引出事与愿违的结果，被动结构 be brought back。
annotations.example: He opened the box, only to find it empty.

annotations.phrase: as if she were reporting the weather
annotations.meaning: 就像她在播报天气一样
annotations.explain: as if + 虚拟语气描写不真实的比较，反衬她异常平静。
annotations.example: He spoke as if he knew everything.

annotations.phrase: Who was I supposed to tell
annotations.explain: be supposed to 表示通常的要求、合理预期；反问凸显无人求助。
annotations.example: Who am I supposed to contact?

annotations.explain: 前后约定未完成前仍可改变选择；与原版 back out 不同。
annotations.example: You can change your mind tomorrow.

annotations.explain: make sth clear 用于提出清晰条件。
annotations.example: Let me make one thing clear.

annotations.explain: keep a promise = 履行承诺，不能承诺的事情不应轻易保证。
annotations.example: Don't make promises you can't keep.

annotations.explain: until 表示截止到触发事件的时间点；旧版 cut short by 不再出现。
annotations.example: The peace lasted only until noon.

annotations.phrase: drew a sheet of paper from her sleeve
annotations.explain: draw sth from + 位置 表示取出；与 tucked into 不同。
annotations.example: He drew a letter from his pocket.

annotations.explain: freely 强调自主意愿；consent to sth / consent to do sth。
annotations.example: She never freely consented to the arrangement.

annotations.phrase: can't tell everyone I married him happily
annotations.meaning: 不能向外宣称我心甘情愿嫁了他
annotations.explain: 指对外表述的边界，不表示纸张可以自动撤销婚姻。
annotations.example: You can't tell everyone I agreed.

annotations.explain: go back on one's word，违背此前承诺。
annotations.example: I won't go back on my word.

annotations.explain: give sth to sb 是普通交付；不再是旧版 entrust 的原文。
annotations.example: I gave the documents to Mia.

annotations.explain: hold sth against sb 是因为旧事迁怒/记恨。
annotations.example: Please don't hold the mistake against me.

annotations.explain: let go 与 let sb go 的结构不同。
annotations.example: Let go of the rope.

annotations.explain: 根据宾语及情境决定是处理事务还是照顾人。
annotations.example: I need to take care of a few things.

annotations.explain: end / break off 根据情境，旧版 break off this marriage 不再逐字出现。
annotations.example: They decided to end the engagement.

annotations.explain: come back to sb 指回忆重新出现，不是人返回。
annotations.example: The answer came back to me later.

annotations.phrase: barely pushed the blade an inch
annotations.explain: barely 表示几乎没有或仅仅；此处强调拔出很少。
annotations.example: She barely opened the door.

annotations.explain: 私人账目被指与官方记录不一致；不等于证实犯罪。
annotations.example: The dates don't match.

annotations.explain: lose one's composure 是情绪或神态失控，比生气更具体。
annotations.example: He lost his composure during the meeting.

annotations.phrase: needed Xie Linzhou to waste his time here
annotations.meaning: 需要谢临舟在这里耗费时间
annotations.explain: need sb to do 表示需要某人做某事；此处是叙述者推断温梨用替嫁拖延时间。
annotations.example: We needed him to wait outside.

annotations.explain: connected to 表示关联，不能推导认罪或已判定事实。
annotations.example: The files connected to the case were sealed.

annotations.explain: for the time being 与 forever 不同，表示过渡安排。
annotations.example: Stay here for the time being.

annotations.explain: be named in 文件仅表示出现名字，不能直接推断有罪。
annotations.example: The company is named in the report.

annotations.meaning: 我的问题里最不重要的一桩
annotations.explain: the smallest of + 复数，表示相对程度；新版已无 turn out to be。
annotations.example: That delay was the smallest of our problems.
